title: Mikaela Naylon Give Kids a Chance Act
official_title: To amend the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act with respect to molecularly targeted pediatric cancer investigations, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: Republican sponsor with 313 cosponsors — well over half the House signed on across both parties — and House passage came by voice vote under suspension of the rules, a consensus track. No organized opposition to the pediatric-study or voucher provisions appears in the metadata; the main risk is Senate floor time rather than substantive resistance.
summary: Requires drug companies to study whether their targeted adult cancer drugs work in children — including when used in combination with other cancer drugs — and lets FDA seek penalties from companies that skip required pediatric studies without a good-faith effort. It also extends the rare pediatric disease priority review voucher program through September 30, 2029, modernizes the organ transplant network, and raises the Medicare Improvement Fund from $1.40B to $2.62B.
brief: Extends required pediatric cancer studies to combination therapies, extends the rare pediatric disease priority review voucher program through September 30, 2029, and raises the Medicare Improvement Fund from $1.40B to $2.62B.

sections.label: Sections 2-4 — Pediatric Study Requirements and Enforcement

items.main: Expands required molecularly targeted pediatric cancer investigations so they can cover the application drug used in combination with other active ingredients — either standard-of-care pediatric cancer ingredients or the sponsor's own approved adult cancer ingredients directed at a molecular target relevant to a pediatric cancer.
items.detail: Investigations must be designed to yield clinically meaningful pediatric data on dosing, safety, and preliminary efficacy, using age-appropriate formulations. Combination investigations may be required only for drugs with a single new active ingredient, or for unapproved combinations of ingredients each previously approved for adult cancer. The changes apply to applications submitted 3 years or more after enactment; FDA must issue draft implementation guidance within 12 months.

items.main: Allows FDA to pursue penalty action under section 303 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act against sponsors who fail pediatric-study requirements — but only after finding the sponsor demonstrated a lack of due diligence.
items.detail: Prior law expressly excluded pediatric-study noncompliance from section 303 action. FDA must first issue a noncompliance letter, give the sponsor 45 days to respond in writing, and review the response before making a due-diligence determination. No enforcement is allowed for drugs no longer marketed, and only failures occurring 180 days or more after enactment can be pursued.

items.main: Adds to FDA's annual PREA-tracking report an evaluation of compliance with deferral deadlines and a public listing of every penalty, settlement, or payment for pediatric-study noncompliance, naming the drug, its sponsor, and the amount.
items.detail: The listing is added to the report required under section 508(b) of the Food and Drug Administration Safety and Innovation Act.

sections.label: Sections 5-7 — Rare and Pediatric Disease Incentives

items.main: Extends FDA's authority to award rare pediatric disease priority review vouchers through September 30, 2029, replacing the December 20, 2024 cutoff.
items.detail: Under the program, a sponsor that wins approval of a rare pediatric disease product receives a voucher entitling the holder to a 6-month priority FDA review of a later drug application; vouchers may be transferred or sold without limit. The bill also makes the priority-review user fee due when the voucher is actually used, and orders a GAO study of the program's effectiveness with findings due within 5 years.

items.main: Narrows orphan-drug exclusivity: the 7-year exclusive-approval window now blocks competitors only for the same approved use or indication within the rare disease, instead of the same disease or condition.
items.detail: The change applies to every drug designated as an orphan drug, regardless of when it was designated or approved.

items.main: Authorizes $25M for each of fiscal years 2026 through 2028 for the Public Health Service Act program for pediatric studies of drugs.
items.detail: Amends section 409I(d)(1) of the Public Health Service Act, which funds pediatric studies of drugs that still need testing in children.

sections.label: Sections 8-9 — Transplant Network and an FDA Office Abroad

items.main: Modernizes the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network: encourages electronic health-record integration for automated donor referrals, allows a 24-hour telephone or information technology service, and calls for considering a public transplant-statistics dashboard.
items.detail: The Secretary may also collect registration fees from network members for each transplant candidate listed — usable only to support network operations, with per-member amounts and uses posted publicly each quarter. The fee authority expires 3 years after enactment, and GAO must review the fee program within 2 years.

items.main: Creates an Abraham Accords Office within FDA, to be located in an Abraham Accords country within two years of enactment.
items.detail: The office will provide technical assistance to regulatory partners in Abraham Accords countries — including on good manufacturing practices — and facilitate interactions between FDA and interested parties there. HHS must report to Congress on the office's results within 3 years.

sections.label: Sections 10-11 — Generic Drug Transparency and Medicare Fund

items.main: Requires FDA, on request, to tell a generic-drug applicant whether its product is qualitatively and quantitatively the same as the brand-name listed drug — and if not, to identify the differing ingredients and the amount of any quantitative deviation.
items.detail: Once FDA determines a generic matches, it cannot change that determination after the application is filed except for a safety-based formulation change in the listed drug or a written error finding with notice to the applicant. Draft guidance is due within one year of enactment.

items.main: Raises the Medicare Improvement Fund from $1.40B to $2.62B.
items.detail: Amends section 1898(b)(1) of the Social Security Act to increase the amount available to the Secretary for improvements to the original Medicare program.

underreported.summary: Increases the Medicare Improvement Fund from $1.40B to $2.62B by amending the Social Security Act.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's title and stated subject are pediatric cancer drug investigations; this provision changes a Medicare fund balance and is unrelated to drug studies.

underreported.summary: Establishes a new FDA office physically located in an Abraham Accords country to provide regulatory technical assistance and facilitate industry interactions there.
underreported.why_unreported: A foreign-based FDA office serving international regulatory cooperation is a different subject from the pediatric-drug provisions named in the bill's title.

underreported.section: Section 3 — Ensuring Completion of Pediatric Study Requirements
underreported.summary: Strikes the clause that shielded pediatric-study noncompliance from section 303 penalty action and replaces it with penalty exposure whenever the sponsor lacked due diligence.
underreported.why_unreported: The section label reads as administrative housekeeping, but the operative text reverses a prior statutory exemption from penalties.

gaps: The bill authorizes $25M a year for pediatric drug studies only through fiscal 2028, while the voucher authority it extends runs through September 30, 2029.
Sponsors get a 45-day window to respond to a noncompliance letter, but the bill sets no deadline for FDA to act after reviewing the response.
The transplant-statistics dashboard is only something the network must consider establishing; the bill does not require it or set a deadline.
The Abraham Accords Office must be established within two years, but the bill provides no dedicated appropriation for the office or its staffing.
FDA must answer generic applicants' sameness requests, but the bill sets no deadline for providing that answer.

added: Combination-therapy pediatric cancer investigations — required studies may cover the application drug used with standard-of-care or same-sponsor adult cancer ingredients

Abraham Accords Office within FDA, located in an Abraham Accords country within 2 years
Binding FDA sameness determinations for generic-drug formulations, with disclosure of differing ingredients
Transplant-network registration fees (3-year authority) with quarterly public posting of amounts and uses
$25M per year authorized for pediatric drug studies for fiscal years 2026 through 2028
modified: Rare pediatric disease priority review voucher authority — award cutoff moved from December 20, 2024 to September 30, 2029
Orphan-drug 7-year exclusivity — narrowed from the same disease or condition to the same approved use or indication
Priority-review user fee — now due when the voucher is used, upon submission of the application
removed: Statutory exclusion that kept pediatric-study noncompliance outside section 303 penalty action
